variants.name: SQLAlchemy version counter
variants.implementation_notes: SQLAlchemy's mapper supports a version id column directly: map a NOT NULL integer column and set __mapper_args__ = {'version_id_col': version_id}; the ORM then emits UPDATE ... WHERE id = :id AND version_id = :old while incrementing the counter, and raises sqlalchemy.orm.exc.StaleDataError when zero rows matched. A version_id_generator callable (GUID, timestamp, or the server-side PostgreSQL xmin with version_id_generator=False) replaces the default integer counting. The feature applies to the ORM flush path only - multirow update()/delete() statements never check the token, as the documentation warns.
pitfalls: Versioning only guards the flush path: session.execute(update(...)) and Query.update() emit bulk statements with no version check.
A server-side generator needs RETURNING-capable backends, otherwise SQLAlchemy issues an extra SELECT per write and can miss a concurrent bump.
A NULL version column is unsupported - the column must be NOT NULL, including for rows that existed before the column was added.

variants.name: Django conditional queryset update
variants.implementation_notes: Django's ORM has no version support, so the guard is expressed with it: filter the queryset by the expected version and issue update() with the new values plus version=F('version') + 1; update() returns the number of rows matched, so 0 is the conflict signal - the same guarded statement as in raw SQL, in ORM form. Django's own answer for the pessimistic case is select_for_update(), which locks the rows for the duration of the surrounding atomic block.
variants.code_sketch:
updated = (Account.objects
           .filter(pk=pk, version=expected)
           .update(balance=new_balance, version=F("version") + 1))
if updated == 0:
    raise StaleAccount()      # re-read, merge or retry
# note: select_for_update() is the pessimistic alternative, not this check
pitfalls: version=F('version') + 1 must be evaluated by the database; computing version + 1 in Python writes the stale value back and recreates the lost update.
select_for_update() has no effect outside a transaction (autocommit), so as a 'lock' it silently does nothing unless it runs inside transaction.atomic().
model.save() never compares versions - the optimistic check must live in the conditional update, not in save().
